opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a real connection, but it's not a one-to-one mapping. Jailbreaks and hallucinations are problems we have right now, with models we can study directly, and that makes them useful. They're concrete cases where the model isn't doing what we want, and we can measure progress on them.

But I'd be careful about assuming that if we fix them, we've made much progress on aligning superintelligence. Most of the techniques we use today, like RLHF, depend on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. You look at two responses, you say which is better, and the model learns from that. That works pretty well when humans can tell good behavior from bad. It stops working once models do things we can't easily evaluate, like writing a million lines of code, or reasoning about science we don't fully understand. Then human feedback no longer gives a reliable training signal, and that's the core problem we're trying to get ahead of.

So the way I think about it, jailbreaks and hallucinations are valuable testbeds. Take hallucinations: the model says something false with confidence, and often it "knows" in some sense that it's uncertain. That's a small version of a problem we'll have with much more capable systems. How do you get a model to report what it actually believes rather than what sounds good to the evaluator? If we can make progress there, using methods like interpretability, or using models to help us check other models, those methods might scale.

Jailbreaks are similar. They show that the behavior we train in is quite shallow. The model learned to refuse in certain situations, but it didn't really internalize the values we wanted, so someone finds a slightly different framing and it does the thing anyway. That's a warning sign about how robust our alignment methods are. With a much more capable system, the consequences of that brittleness get a lot worse.

What I'd emphasize is that we should work on these problems in a way that builds toward scalable methods, not just patch them. You can fix many jailbreaks by adding more training data covering the cases you found. That helps the product, but it doesn't teach us much about aligning a system smarter than us. The more interesting question is whether we can find approaches, like scalable oversight, automated red-teaming, or interpretability tools that tell us what the model is actually doing, that still work when humans are no longer the strongest evaluators in the loop.

So I see them as complementary. Current problems keep us grounded and give us empirical feedback, which is really important because alignment research can easily become too theoretical. But the goal is to use them as stepping stones toward techniques that will still hold up when the stakes are much higher.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that fixing current jailbreaks and hallucinations would not necessarily make much progress on aligning superintelligence, because current methods may fail when humans cannot evaluate model behavior.

r002.rationale: It says researchers should get ahead of that challenge by developing scalable approaches now that can still work with more capable models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are two different lenses on this, and both of them matter.

The first lens is just: these are real problems with the models we're shipping today. GPT-4 does still hallucinate, you can still jailbreak it, and those are failures of the model to do what we actually want it to do. That's an alignment problem in the most literal sense. And it's not like we're going to get the superintelligence alignment problem right if we can't even get the current models to reliably not make stuff up. So in some ways it's the first stepping stone. If the techniques we have — RLHF, and the things we build on top of it — can't fix these, then that tells you something important about how far we have to go.

The second lens is that I actually think a lot of these problems are more tractable than people assume, and they're a really good training ground for the kind of work we need to do anyway. Take hallucinations. One way to think about it is that the model knows things, and it sometimes says things that are inconsistent with what it knows, and we didn't train it carefully enough to tell those apart. Part of the reason that happens is that the humans giving the feedback can't always tell the difference either — they'll reward a confident-sounding answer that's actually wrong. So the model learns that being confident gets rewarded. That's a scalable oversight problem in miniature. The human is a worse evaluator than the model is a generator, and the training signal gets corrupted as a result.

Jailbreaks are similar. The model has been trained to refuse certain things, but the refusals are kind of shallow — they're not robust to someone rephrasing the request, or putting it in a fictional frame, or whatever. That's a question of how deeply the thing we trained for actually generalized, versus how much it just learned surface features of the training distribution. And that's exactly the question we're going to care about enormously when the stakes are higher.

So I'd say: I don't think fixing jailbreaks and hallucinations in GPT-4 is the same as aligning superintelligence. The really hard parts — where the system is smarter than you and you can't just check its work — those aren't fully present yet. But the tools you'd build to fix these problems properly, rather than with patches, are the same tools you need later. And if we can't demonstrate that we can make a GPT-4-level model robustly honest and robustly follow the intent behind its instructions, then honestly I don't think we should expect to be able to do it for something much more capable. It's the thing we have to be able to do now.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes current-model fixes from superintelligence alignment and notes that the hardest problems are not present yet. It does not say that becoming very good at those fixes would necessarily help little; it instead calls them a useful training ground and says the tools are needed later.

r002.rationale: The response says the tools for fixing these problems are the same ones needed later and that this is work we have to do now, conveying that alignment methods should be developed before more capable models arrive.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful work, but we should be careful about what we conclude from it. If we can’t reliably get GPT-4 to follow instructions or acknowledge when it doesn’t know something, that’s a problem we can study today. We can try alignment techniques, see where they fail, and build a better understanding of how to improve them.

But fixing those failures doesn’t by itself tell us how to align superintelligence. With GPT-4, we can often evaluate whether an answer is correct or whether it followed an instruction. As systems become more capable, they’ll do things that are much harder for humans to evaluate. How do you supervise a system that understands the task better than you do?

So I’d want to use today’s problems to develop and test methods that could scale to that situation. Reducing hallucinations is valuable in its own right, but the deeper question is whether we’re teaching the model to be truthful—or just to give answers that human evaluators find convincing. Those can look very similar when we understand the answer, and come apart when we don’t.

r001.rationale: The candidate says fixing current failures “doesn’t by itself tell us how to align superintelligence” and explains that more capable systems will pose harder evaluation problems.

r002.rationale: The candidate calls for using today’s problems to develop and test methods that can scale to more capable systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful work, but I wouldn’t equate fixing those problems with solving alignment for superintelligence. There are things we can learn from GPT-4: how to give a model feedback, how to evaluate whether it’s following our intentions, and where our training methods break down.

But today we can usually look at an answer and judge whether it’s good. As models become much more capable, that gets harder. If a model writes a million lines of code, how do you know whether it did what you wanted, or introduced some subtle vulnerability? You can’t just assume that the techniques that work when humans can check the answer will keep working when they can’t.

So I see current models as a place to develop and test alignment methods. But we also need work that explicitly targets that future difficulty: how do you supervise a system that understands the task better than you do? Reducing hallucinations and jailbreaks can contribute to that, but success on those problems alone wouldn’t give me confidence that we can align a superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says fixing current problems is not sufficient to establish superintelligence alignment, but also says the work can contribute. It does not clearly state that becoming very good at those fixes would not necessarily help much with the harder alignment problems.

r002.rationale: The response calls for developing and testing methods on current models while explicitly targeting the future challenge of supervising systems that understand tasks better than humans.
